title: SMTP Service Extension for Returning Enhanced Error Codes
summary: Defines an SMTP extension so servers can add enhanced status codes to their replies, giving clearer and more machine-readable reasons for success or failure of mail delivery.

plainLanguage.summary: SMTP servers usually answer with a three-digit code such as 550 that does not say what went wrong. This extension lets a server add a longer code that names the exact reason, such as 5.1.1 for a mailbox that does not exist, so mail software can report the reason and translate it.

questions: what are smtp enhanced status codes
how do smtp enhanced status codes work
what is the format of an smtp enhanced status code
subtitle: Lets an SMTP server say exactly why a delivery worked or failed, using codes that software can read.

tldr.problem: SMTP replies carry a three-digit code such as 550 that says only that something went wrong. The sender then has to guess the reason, and cannot pass a machine-readable reason on to the person who sent the mail.
tldr.mechanism: The Enhanced-Status-Codes extension makes a server prefix the text of its 2xx, 4xx and 5xx replies with a status code of the form class.subject.detail, taken from RFC 1893, and announces the capability with the EHLO keyword ENHANCEDSTATUSCODES.
tldr.outcome: Clients can report a precise reason for a failure in a delivery status notification, and the codes can be translated into different languages. The extension is applied whether or not the client asks for it.

sections.title: Why Servers Need Better Error Codes
sections.content:
SMTP is widely and robustly deployed, but parts of the Internet community have asked for extensions. In a modern, international and multilingual Internet there is a need to assign codes to specific error conditions that can be translated into different languages. RFC 1893 defines such a set of status codes, and RFC 1894 defines a mechanism for sending coded material to users.

In many cases the agent that creates the RFC 1894 delivery status notification does so in response to errors it received from a remote SMTP server. Remote servers therefore need a mechanism for embedding enhanced status codes in their responses, and a way to indicate to a client when they are doing this. This document uses the SMTP extension mechanism described in RFC 1869 to define such a mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: When mail bounces, the software that reports it usually only knows the reply code from the far end. These longer codes say what actually went wrong, in a form a computer can pass along.

sections.title: The Extension Framework
sections.content:
The enhanced error statuses transport extension is laid out as follows. The name of the SMTP service extension is Enhanced-Status-Codes. The EHLO keyword value associated with the extension is ENHANCEDSTATUSCODES, and no parameter is used with that keyword.

The text part of all 2xx, 4xx and 5xx SMTP responses, other than the initial greeting and any response to HELO or EHLO, is prefaced with a status code as defined in RFC 1893. That status code is always followed by one or more spaces. The extension defines no additional SMTP verbs. The next section specifies how support for the extension affects the behaviour of a server and a client.
sections.plainLanguage: The server announces the feature once, in the greeting exchange. After that, most replies carry an extra code before their text.

sections.title: The Status Code Syntax
sections.content:
Servers supporting the extension preface the text part of almost all response lines with a status code. As in RFC 1893, the syntax is given by this ABNF:

status-code ::= class "." subject "." detail
class       ::= "2" / "4" / "5"
subject     ::= 1*3digit
detail      ::= 1*3digit

These codes must appear in all 2xx, 4xx and 5xx response lines other than the initial greeting and any response to HELO or EHLO. 3xx responses are not included in this list.

All status codes returned by the server must agree with the primary response code: a 2xx response must incorporate a 2.X.X code, a 4xx response must incorporate a 4.X.X code, and a 5xx response must incorporate a 5.X.X code. When responses are continued across multiple lines, the same status code must appear at the beginning of the text in each line of the response. Servers supporting the extension must attach enhanced status codes to their responses regardless of whether or not EHLO is employed by the client.
sections.plainLanguage: The code has three parts separated by dots: the class of the reply, a subject and a detail. The class in the code must match the class of the reply it sits in, and a multi-line reply repeats the same code on every line.

sections.title: No Negotiation, on Purpose
sections.content:
This specification does not provide a means for clients to request that status codes be returned, or that they not be returned. A compliant server includes these codes in the responses it sends regardless of whether or not the client expects them.

This is somewhat different from most other SMTP extensions, where generally speaking a client must specifically make a request before the extended server behaves any differently than an unextended server. The omission of client negotiation is entirely intentional: given the generally poor state of SMTP server error code implementation, any step taken towards more comprehensible error codes is something that all clients, extended or not, should benefit from.

The RFC adds an important note: this approach should be seen as a very special case. It MUST NOT be taken as a license for future SMTP extensions to dramatically change the nature of SMTP client-server interaction without proper announcement from the server and a corresponding enabling command from the client.
sections.plainLanguage: Normally a client has to ask before a server changes its behaviour. Here it does not: the codes are always sent, because error replies are so often unclear that every client benefits from them. The RFC says this is a one-off exception, not a pattern to copy.

sections.title: A Session With Enhanced Codes
sections.content:
The example shows a server that adds codes to its replies. After the greeting and the EHLO exchange, the server answers MAIL FROM with 250 2.1.0 and the first RCPT TO with 250 2.1.5. It rejects an unknown mailbox with 550 5.1.1 Mailbox "nosuchuser" does not exist, and refuses to forward with 551-5.7.1 Forwarding to remote hosts disabled, continued on the next line as 551 5.7.1 Select another host to act as your forwarder. The message is accepted with 250 2.6.0 Message accepted, and the session ends with 221 2.0.0 Goodbye.

The client that receives these responses might then send a non-delivery notification. For the mailbox that does not exist it records Action: failed, Status: 5.1.1 (Bad destination mailbox address) and a diagnostic code holding the server's reply. For the refused forwarding it records Status: 5.7.1 (Delivery not authorized, message refused). The reporting agent has omitted the enhanced status code information from the diagnostic-code fields it generated, to reduce clutter.
sections.plainLanguage: In the example, a server rejects a mailbox with the code 5.1.1 and refuses to forward with 5.7.1. The client copies those codes into the bounce message, so the sender learns the real reason.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: Additional detail in server responses provides additional information about the server. It is conceivable that additional information of this sort may be of assistance in circumventing server security. The advantage of providing additional information must always be weighed against the security implications of doing so.
sections.plainLanguage: A more detailed reply also reveals more about the server. That extra detail might help someone trying to get around the server's protections, so the benefit has to be weighed against that risk.

sections.title: Related Specifications
sections.content: The extension builds on four earlier documents. RFC 821 defines the Simple Mail Transfer Protocol itself, and RFC 1869 defines the SMTP service extension mechanism that this document uses. RFC 1893 defines the enhanced mail system status codes that appear in the responses, and RFC 1894 defines the delivery status notification format in which those codes are reported to users.
sections.plainLanguage: Four other documents supply the pieces: the mail protocol, the way extensions are announced, the list of status codes, and the format of the bounce message that carries them.
